facts.text: Waterloo’s original name, Bellefontaine, means “beautiful spring,” chosen for the water source that French travelers used between Cahokia and Kaskaskia.
In 1816 Emery Peters Rogers arrived from Massachusetts and, four years later, opened the first permanent store, mill, and quarry that sparked the town’s growth.

Legend says that in 1818 Irishman Charles Carroll built a house and barn on opposite sides of the creek and declared, “It won’t be Bellefontaine, and it won’t be Peterstown, but begorra, I’ll give ye’s both your Waterloo.”.
The Peterstown House, still standing, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1977 and remains a tangible link to Waterloo’s early settlers.
Waterloo sits on a ridge that drains east to Prairie du Long Creek and west to Fountain Creek, protecting it from the frequent flooding that plagued the lower Mississippi Valley.
The town lies along the historic trail that connected Kaskaskia to St. Louis, making it a key stop for early travelers moving westward.
